name: Rafael Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, not the poles on your street. We go where the project is, which right now is a new 230-kilovolt line going across the hills north of the river, so Monday to Thursday I'm in a motel with a hot plate. A good day is clipping in at the top of a tower with the whole valley under you and getting a stretch of conductor hung clean. A bad day is waiting four hours in the truck because the wind's too strong to go up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the life around that like, being away so much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Lucía teaches second grade back home, and we're saving to get married, maybe in a couple of years. I call her every night from the motel parking lot because the signal's better there. I cook rice and beans on the hot plate for me and Kwame, the guy I room with, because otherwise it's gas-station sandwiches all week. The pay's good with the travel allowance, and I've got maybe four months of expenses put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, "See, they were overselling it," and leave it there. I'm not someone who posts much. Maybe a joke in the crew chat about the robots not showing up for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, which is fine by me. The work's hard on the body but it's steady and it pays. I'd keep my head down and keep saving for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep travelling with the project, keep putting a bit from every travel allowance into the wedding fund. I use an AI app now and then to tidy up emails to the landlord, I'd probably keep doing that and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit like hearing a storm went the other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of that "routine stuff" already show up on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Our foreman uses something on his tablet to write up the daily reports, and the engineers use software to plan where the towers go. And last year they flew a drone to pull the first light rope between two towers instead of a helicopter. That was cool to watch, I'll admit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, where do you see yourself in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still up there, hopefully running my own small crew. Maybe off the road a bit more, once we're married, doing local substation or distribution work so I'm home at night. That's the plan, anyway.

S0.say: I'd say they were overselling it and leave it at that. I don't post much, maybe a joke in the crew chat about robots not turning up for work.
S0.think: For me it means nothing changes, which suits me fine. The work is hard on the body but it's steady and it pays for the wedding we're saving for.
S0.do: Keeps travelling with the transmission project and keeps putting part of every travel allowance into the wedding fund. Carries on using an AI app now and then for emails, and nothing more.
S0.feel: Calm, like hearing a storm went the other way.
S0.quote: I'd probably say, "See, they were overselling it," and leave it there.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is easygoing and low-key, a lineworker more interested in the wedding fund than the news. He's seen a drone pull a pilot rope between towers and admits it impressed him. His five-year plan is about coming off the road, not about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, this has happened before, the helicopters came in and we still needed guys on the towers. People adjust if the company does it right. I'd also say the union needs to be at the table, because "done right" doesn't happen by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, but the guys I room with might not be. The drones and the robot arms would take the easiest parts first, the stuff they give the newer guys. I'm in the middle, so I'd have to make sure I'm the one who knows how to run the new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw other crews using the new equipment without problems, I'd sign up for whatever training the company offered on it, drone operation or the line robots. I'd probably start using the AI on my phone more for reading manuals, the way Kwame already does. And I'd go to the union meetings instead of skipping them for the motel bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's the kind of uneasy where you know what to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "the company" would decide. What would you want the union to push for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training paid for by the company, on company time, not on our weekends. And no cutting crew sizes just because a drone does part of the job. Same pay for the people who learn the new kit, or better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Lucía's job is pretty safe in this one, kids still need teachers. We'd keep the date.

S1.say: I'd say this has happened before: helicopters came in and we still needed people on towers. People adjust if the company does it right, and the union has to be at the table to make sure it does.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd be fine, but newer guys might not be, because machines take the easy parts first. I'm in the middle, so I'd need to be the one who knows the new gear.
S1.do: Signs up for company training on drones or line robots once he sees other crews using them without trouble. Uses AI on his phone more to read manuals and starts attending union meetings regularly.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but the kind where he knows what to do about it.
S1.quote: The drones and the robot arms would take the easiest parts first, the stuff they give the newer guys.
S1.fieldNote: Typical of his steady temperament, he'd wait to see the equipment proven on other crews before training on it. His progressive side shows in wanting company-paid training on company time and no cuts to crew size. He keeps the wedding date, which tells me he doesn't see a real threat yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, fast, with real money for working people, because the companies won't. I'd say it at work and I'd probably finally post something. This isn't a thing you can leave to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Two years is not enough time to retrain, and if robots can hang conductor, a transmission crew is a big expensive line on somebody's budget. I'd be one of a lot of guys looking for the same few jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd stop the travel spending, cook every meal, and push the savings from four months to six. I'd sit down with Lucía and talk about pushing the wedding back. I'd sign up with the union's hardship fund and any government programme, no pride about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being up on a tower when the weather turns and you can't get down quick enough. Tight in the chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the wedding in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd postpone it, I think. Not cancel, just wait until we know what's coming. Her mother would be upset, she's already picked the church, but Lucía's practical. She'd say a wedding is one day and rent is every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should step in. What would that look like for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guaranteed income for a while, enough to cover rent, and free retraining. And keep the power companies public, or at least make them keep people on until there's something else. The lights still need to stay on, and I'd want someone accountable for that who isn't a robot.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in fast with real money for working people, because companies won't. I'd probably finally post something about it.
S2.think: Honestly it scares me. Two years isn't enough to retrain, and a transmission crew is a big expensive line on someone's budget, so I'd be competing with many others for a few jobs.
S2.do: Stops travel spending, cooks every meal and pushes savings from four to six months. Talks with Lucía about postponing the wedding and signs up for the union hardship fund and any government programme.
S2.feel: Tight in the chest, like being caught on a tower when the weather turns.
S2.quote: She'd say a wedding is one day and rent is every month.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Rafael's calm cracks: the speed leaves no room for his usual wait-and-learn approach. He'd postpone the wedding, and Lucía is the practical anchor in his story. His politics come through clearly here, with guaranteed income and public ownership of utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd be telling people at work, don't wait, get the union to fight for retraining money now. I'd say it calmly, though, because nobody listens to the guy who's shouting. Five years is enough to do something if we start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I'd have to get off the towers and into something that works with the robots, like maintaining them or supervising them. That's realistic in five years. In two, it's not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait maybe a year to see which machines the company actually buys, then get certified on them. I'd keep saving and probably still get married, just a smaller wedding, at Lucía's parents' place instead of the hall. I'd go to a couple of protests if the union called them, and I'd vote for whoever promises real retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but I'd be watching every announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is having five years different from two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, you just survive. Five, you can make a plan and actually follow it. It's the difference between jumping off a tower and climbing down it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kwame, if he asked you what to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him what my uncle told me when the factory closed back home: learn the new machine before they bring it in, not after. Kwame's quicker with tech than me, actually, so he'd probably be telling me.

S3.say: I'd tell people at work not to wait and to get the union fighting for retraining money now. I'd say it calmly, because five years is enough to do something if we start.
S3.think: I think I'd have to get off the towers and into work alongside the robots, maintaining or supervising them. That's realistic in five years, not in two.
S3.do: Waits about a year to see which machines the company buys, then gets certified on them. Keeps saving, holds a smaller wedding at Lucía's parents' place, joins union protests and votes for real retraining.
S3.feel: Anxious, but less than the fast version, and watching every announcement.
S3.quote: It's the difference between jumping off a tower and climbing down it.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turns panic into a plan for Rafael: wait a year, see what's bought, then certify. The wedding goes ahead but smaller. His uncle's factory closure is clearly a story he carries around as a lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's manageable if we don't waste it. Ten years is enough to train a whole generation of lineworkers to do something else, or to run the machines. But only if somebody actually pays for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd be thirty-seven, still young enough to learn, old enough to know what I want. What worries me is whether the work that's left pays like this does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it slowly. Keep working, get married on schedule, and in a few years once I see what's working for other guys, train for robot maintenance or grid control. I'd join the union's committee on new technology so I hear things early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still the same ending, but ten years feels like a road, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what happens to the plan you had of coming off the road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still happens, just maybe sooner. If I'm going to retrain anyway, I might as well do it into something local, like the control room in town. Then I'm home for dinner and Lucía doesn't marry a motel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently in your own spending or plans with a decade's warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not buy a house too early, rent a few more years. And maybe not have kids until I knew where I'd land. That's a big thing to say, but with ten years you have to think about it.

S4.say: I'd say this one is manageable if we don't waste it. Ten years is enough to train a generation of lineworkers to run the machines or do something else, if someone pays for it.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd be all right at thirty-seven, young enough to learn. What worries me is whether the work that's left pays as well as this does.
S4.do: Keeps working and marries on schedule, then retrains for robot maintenance or grid control once he sees what works for others. Joins the union's technology committee and holds off on buying a house or having children.
S4.feel: Uneasy; ten years feels like a road, not a cliff.
S4.quote: If I'm going to retrain anyway, I might as well do it into something local, like the control room in town.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Rafael folds the change into his existing plan to come off the road. His concern shifts from losing work to whether the new work pays as well. He surprised me by raising holding off on children, which he said was a big thing to admit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, for sure, because there's no time to do anything right. What would help is real retraining money that starts before the jobs go, and some kind of income guarantee for a year or two while people learn. And the union being in the room when they decide what to buy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the families. Everyone asks what the worker would do, but Lucía would be the one holding things together if I lost the job. That's not a small thing.

headlineQuote: Then I'm home for dinner and Lucía doesn't marry a motel.
portrait: Rafael Reyes is a 27-year-old transmission lineworker who spends Monday to Thursday in a motel on a new high-voltage project, cooking rice and beans on a hot plate. He's saving to marry Lucía, a primary teacher, and has about four months of expenses put away. Easygoing and pro-union, he likes new equipment once he's seen it proven on other crews. He's calm about the mild pictures, alarmed by AGI in two years, and with more warning he turns the change into his existing plan to come off the road and work closer to home.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to do anything properly.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining money that starts before jobs go, an income guarantee for a year or two while people learn, and the union in the room when equipment is chosen.
